subject: science
title: Chemistry — Atoms, elements and compounds
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Chemistry — Atoms, elements and compounds, KS3 Science (National Curriculum).
meta_desc: KS3 Science practice covering Chemistry — Atoms, elements and compounds, from the National Curriculum programme of study.
final_note: You worked through Chemistry — Atoms, elements and compounds: 4 programme-of-study statements.

concepts.def: The smallest particle of an element that can exist. Atoms are far too small to see, even with a light microscope: a grain of powder you can see contains a huge number of them. A single atom does not have the properties of a lump of the substance, such as its colour or hardness.

A simple model of matter put forward by John Dalton in the early 1800s. In Dalton's model: everything is made of tiny atoms that cannot be broken down; all the atoms of one element are identical, and atoms of different elements are different (they have different masses); atoms join in fixed whole-number ratios to make compounds; in a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed. It is a model: it pictures each atom as a tiny solid sphere so that we can explain what we observe.

A change in which new substances are made. The atoms in the starting substances (reactants) are rearranged: they separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways in the products. No atoms are created or destroyed.

A substance made of only one type of atom. An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical reaction. Some elements are made of atoms that are not joined in molecules (helium, He; iron, Fe); others are made of molecules containing two atoms of that one element (oxygen, O₂; nitrogen, N₂; hydrogen, H₂; chlorine, Cl₂).
concepts.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds

concepts.def: A particle made of two or more atoms chemically joined (bonded) together. The atoms can be of the same element, as in O₂ and N₂ (elements made of molecules), or of different elements, as in H₂O, CO₂ and CH₄ (compounds made of molecules).
concepts.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds

concepts.def: A substance made of atoms of two or more different elements chemically joined (bonded) together in a fixed ratio, for example water, H₂O (2 hydrogen atoms to 1 oxygen atom), and carbon dioxide, CO₂ (1 carbon atom to 2 oxygen atoms). A compound has properties different from those of its elements, and it can be split up only by a chemical reaction.
concepts.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds

concepts.def: Two or more substances (elements or compounds) that are together but not chemically joined. The amounts can vary, each substance keeps its own properties, and the substances can be separated without a chemical reaction. Air, salt water, and iron filings stirred into sulfur powder are mixtures.
concepts.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds

concepts.def: A one- or two-letter code for an element. The first letter is always a capital and a second letter is always lower case: Co is the element cobalt, but CO is carbon (C) and oxygen (O) joined, carbon monoxide. Many symbols come from the English name (H, He, C, N, O, Mg, Al, S, Cl, Ca, Zn); some come from Latin names: Na sodium (natrium), K potassium (kalium), Fe iron (ferrum), Cu copper (cuprum), Ag silver (argentum), Au gold (aurum), Pb lead (plumbum).
concepts.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds

concepts.def: Symbols and numbers that show which elements are in a substance and how many atoms of each there are in one particle (or in what ratio they are joined). Elements made of molecules have formulae (O₂, N₂, H₂, Cl₂) as well as compounds (H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NaCl).
concepts.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds

concepts.def: The small number written after and below a symbol. It counts the atoms of the element just before it; a symbol with no number means one atom. H₂O has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom; C₆H₁₂O₆ has 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 atoms. A large number in front means separate particles: 2N is two separate nitrogen atoms, N₂ is one molecule of two joined nitrogen atoms.
concepts.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds

concepts.def: In a change of state, in dissolving and in a chemical reaction, the total mass stays the same, because the same atoms (particles) are there before and after. Total mass before = total mass after; for a reaction, mass of reactants = mass of products.
concepts.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

concepts.def: Reactants are the substances you start with in a chemical reaction; products are the new substances made. In a word equation an arrow separates them: iron + sulfur → iron sulfide.
concepts.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

concepts.def: A container that nothing can get into or out of, such as a sealed flask or bag. The mass of a sealed container and its contents stays the same whatever change happens inside.
concepts.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

concepts.def: A container open to the air. If a gas is made and escapes, the measured mass goes down; if a gas from the air, such as oxygen, joins on, the measured mass goes up. Total mass is still conserved: the balance simply does not weigh gas that has left or that was in the air before.
concepts.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

concepts.def: When a solid spreads out as separate particles between the particles of a liquid, making a solution. The solid is still there (evaporating the water gives it back), so the mass of the solution = mass of liquid + mass of solid.
concepts.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

concepts.def: Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and subliming (a solid turning straight into a gas). The particles are arranged differently and move differently, but no particles are made or lost, so the mass stays the same.
concepts.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

mcqs.q: Which idea is part of Dalton's atomic model?
options: An atom has the colour of its element
Atoms can be seen with a light microscope
All atoms of one element are identical
Atoms are destroyed when things burn
mcqs.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
mcqs.explain: Yes. In Dalton's model every atom of one element is the same, and atoms of different elements are different (they have different masses). He also said atoms cannot be broken down, made or destroyed.
rationales: You may have thought a copper atom is orange because copper is. In fact colour belongs to a piece of the substance, made of huge numbers of atoms; Dalton's atoms have no colour.
You may have thought atoms are like the tiny cells you see in a microscope. In fact atoms are far too small to see with a light microscope.
Yes. In Dalton's model every atom of one element is the same, and atoms of different elements are different (they have different masses). He also said atoms cannot be broken down, made or destroyed.
You may have thought burning destroys atoms because the fuel seems to vanish. In fact, in Dalton's model atoms are never destroyed; they join with oxygen, and many end up in gases you cannot see.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to make water. In Dalton's model, what happens to the hydrogen atoms?
options: They are destroyed as the hydrogen burns
They become joined to oxygen atoms
They merge with oxygen into water atoms
They become wet, like the water made
mcqs.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
mcqs.explain: Yes. In Dalton's model atoms are rearranged, never made or destroyed, so the hydrogen atoms end up joined to oxygen atoms. Today we know each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
rationales: You may have thought burning destroys the hydrogen because the gas is used up. In fact all the hydrogen atoms are still there, now joined to oxygen atoms in water.

Yes. In Dalton's model atoms are rearranged, never made or destroyed, so the hydrogen atoms end up joined to oxygen atoms. Today we know each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
You may have thought water is made of its own "water atoms". In fact atoms never merge or change in a reaction: in water, hydrogen atoms are joined to oxygen atoms.
You may have thought atoms take on the properties of the substance they are in. In fact wetness belongs to water in bulk, not to single atoms; the hydrogen atoms are simply joined to oxygen atoms.

mcqs.q: Under a school microscope, sulfur powder looks like tiny yellow grains. Which statement about one grain is correct?
options: It is one single atom of sulfur
It is made of atoms that are yellow
It is solid sulfur with no atoms in it
It contains a huge number of atoms
mcqs.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
mcqs.explain: Yes. Atoms are far too small to see, so even a tiny grain contains a huge number of sulfur atoms. The yellow colour belongs to the grain, not to a single atom.
rationales: You may have thought the smallest bit you can see must be one atom. In fact a single atom is far too small to see with a light microscope; each grain contains a huge number of atoms.
You may have thought the atoms must be yellow because the sulfur is. In fact colour is a property of the substance; a single atom is not yellow.
You may have thought a solid grain is just solid stuff all the way through. In fact all matter, solids as well as gases, is made of atoms; each grain contains a huge number of them.
Yes. Atoms are far too small to see, so even a tiny grain contains a huge number of sulfur atoms. The yellow colour belongs to the grain, not to a single atom.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the particles of a substance made from X and Y. Someone makes it again with extra Y. What are its particles like now?
options: One X atom joined to two Y atoms
One X atom joined to more Y atoms
Particles that are mixtures of X and Y
One big new atom formed from X and Y
mcqs.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
mcqs.explain: Yes. In Dalton's model atoms join in a fixed whole-number ratio, so every particle of this compound has one X atom and two Y atoms. Using extra Y does not change that.
rationales: Yes. In Dalton's model atoms join in a fixed whole-number ratio, so every particle of this compound has one X atom and two Y atoms. Using extra Y does not change that.

You may have thought using more Y puts more Y into each particle. In fact the ratio in a compound is fixed: each particle of this compound still has one X atom and two Y atoms. A particle with more Y atoms would be a different compound.
You may have thought two kinds of atom in a particle means it is a mixture. In fact each X atom is joined to two Y atoms in every particle, so this is a compound, not a mixture.
You may have thought the atoms merge into a new kind of atom. In fact, in Dalton's model atoms never merge or change; the X and Y atoms stay separate atoms, joined together.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows elements X and Y reacting to make a compound. Which statement about the compound is correct?
options: It has the properties of both X and Y
Filtering can split it into X and Y
Its ratio of X to Y changes with more X
It has new properties of its own
mcqs.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. A compound is a new substance with properties different from those of its elements. For example, sodium (a reactive metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) make sodium chloride, table salt.
rationales: You may have thought the elements keep their own properties inside the compound. In fact a compound is a new substance, and its properties are different from those of its elements.
You may have thought a compound can be pulled apart like a mixture. In fact the X and Y atoms are chemically joined, so it takes a chemical reaction to split the compound.

You may have thought a compound's make-up depends on how much of each element is used. In fact every particle of this compound has one X atom and one Y atom. A particle with more X atoms would be a different compound.
Yes. A compound is a new substance with properties different from those of its elements. For example, sodium (a reactive metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) make sodium chloride, table salt.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true of every molecule?
options: It contains atoms of two different elements
It is two or more atoms joined together
It is just another word for an atom
It can be seen with a light microscope
mcqs.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. A molecule is two or more atoms joined (bonded) together. The atoms can be the same, as in O₂, or different, as in H₂O.
rationales: You may have thought 'molecule' means 'compound' because H₂O and CO₂ are molecules. In fact an O₂ molecule has two atoms of the same element, oxygen.
Yes. A molecule is two or more atoms joined (bonded) together. The atoms can be the same, as in O₂, or different, as in H₂O.
You may have thought 'atom' and 'molecule' are two words for the same thing. In fact a molecule is made of two or more atoms joined together.
You may have thought a molecule is big enough to see as a speck. In fact molecules, like atoms, are far too small to see with a light microscope.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a compound?
options: Oxygen gas, O₂
Air in a jar
Pure water, H₂O
Salt solution
mcqs.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. Pure water, H₂O, is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen atoms are chemically joined in a fixed ratio of 2 to 1.
rationales: You may have thought oxygen is a compound because it is made of O₂ molecules. In fact both atoms in O₂ are oxygen atoms, so oxygen is an element.
You may have thought air is a compound because it contains several elements. In fact the nitrogen, oxygen and other gases in air are mixed, not joined, so air is a mixture.
Yes. Pure water, H₂O, is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen atoms are chemically joined in a fixed ratio of 2 to 1.
You may have thought salt and water join together when salt dissolves. In fact a salt solution is a mixture: the amount of salt can vary, and evaporating the water gives the salt back.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the particles in a sample of gas. What is the whole sample?
options: An element mixed with a compound
Two compounds mixed together
A compound of two elements
Two elements mixed together
mcqs.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. The pairs of white Y atoms are an element made of molecules, and the X–Y particles are a compound. The two kinds of particle are not joined to each other, so the sample is a mixture of an element and a compound.
rationales: Yes. The pairs of white Y atoms are an element made of molecules, and the X–Y particles are a compound. The two kinds of particle are not joined to each other, so the sample is a mixture of an element and a compound.
You may have thought the Y–Y pairs are a compound because they are molecules. In fact both atoms in each pair are Y atoms, so those particles are an element.
You may have thought anything that contains two elements is a compound. In fact the particles here are not all the same: two different substances are mixed, not joined.
You may have thought two kinds of atom in a sample means a mixture of two elements. In fact each X atom is joined to a Y atom, making a compound, which is mixed with the element Y.

The other three particles are each two small white circles touching. A key below shows the large shaded circle labelled X atom and the small white circle labelled Y atom.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen burns, and oxygen helps things burn. They react to make water, which does neither. What does this show?
options: The atoms were destroyed in the reaction
The atoms changed into new water atoms
Water has too little hydrogen to burn
A new substance with its own properties formed
mcqs.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. Water is a compound, a new substance whose properties are different from those of hydrogen and oxygen. The atoms are the same ones, now joined in a new way.
rationales: You may have thought the hydrogen and oxygen atoms were used up. In fact all the atoms are still there, joined in water molecules; the properties changed because a new substance formed.
You may have thought the atoms turned into a new kind of 'water atom'. In fact atoms do not change: water molecules are hydrogen and oxygen atoms joined together.
You may have thought the hydrogen keeps its properties but there is too little of it. In fact the elements in a compound do not keep their properties; water is a new substance.
Yes. Water is a compound, a new substance whose properties are different from those of hydrogen and oxygen. The atoms are the same ones, now joined in a new way.

mcqs.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
options: Au
Go
AU
Ag
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. Gold's symbol, Au, comes from its Latin name, aurum: a capital first letter, then a lower-case second letter.
rationales: Yes. Gold's symbol, Au, comes from its Latin name, aurum: a capital first letter, then a lower-case second letter.
You may have thought every symbol comes from the English name. In fact some come from Latin names: gold is Au, from aurum.
You may have thought both letters of a symbol are capitals. In fact the second letter is always lower case: AU is wrong, Au is right.
You may have mixed up gold and silver, as both symbols come from Latin and start with A. Ag is silver (argentum); gold is Au (aurum).

mcqs.q: In the formula H₂O, what does the small 2 show?
options: There are two oxygen atoms
There are two of every atom
There are two hydrogen atoms
There are two water molecules
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. The small 2 counts the atom just before it, hydrogen. So H₂O has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
rationales: You may have thought the number counts the atom after it. In fact a small number always counts the atom just before it, so H₂O has one oxygen atom.
You may have thought the 2 doubles everything in the formula. In fact it counts only the hydrogen atoms; there is one oxygen atom.
Yes. The small 2 counts the atom just before it, hydrogen. So H₂O has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
You may have thought a small 2 means two whole molecules, like a big 2 in front. In fact two water molecules would be written 2H₂O; the small 2 counts hydrogen atoms.

mcqs.q: Methane has the formula CH₄. How many atoms are in one molecule of methane?
options: 2 atoms
4 atoms
5 atoms
8 atoms
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. C with no number means one carbon atom, and H₄ means four hydrogen atoms: 1 + 4 = 5.
mcqs.working: C has no number after it, so there is 1 carbon atom. H₄ means 4 hydrogen atoms. Total = 1 + 4 = 5 atoms.
rationales: You may have counted the symbols, C and H. In fact the formula also tells you how many of each atom: 1 carbon + 4 hydrogen = 5.
You may have counted only the atoms with a number. A symbol with no number still counts as one atom, so 1 + 4 = 5.
Yes. C with no number means one carbon atom, and H₄ means four hydrogen atoms: 1 + 4 = 5.
You may have thought the 4 applies to every atom, giving 4 + 4. In fact it counts only the hydrogen atoms before it: 1 + 4 = 5.

mcqs.q: What does the formula N₂ show?
options: Two nitrogen atoms that are not joined up
A compound that contains nitrogen
Two nitrogen atoms joined to each other
A single atom of the element nitrogen
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. N₂ is one molecule made of two nitrogen atoms joined together. Nitrogen gas is an element made of these molecules.
rationales: You may have thought N₂ and 2N mean the same. In fact 2N is two separate atoms; the small 2 in N₂ shows two atoms joined in one molecule.
You may have thought any substance made of molecules is a compound. In fact N₂ has only nitrogen atoms, so it is an element made of molecules.
Yes. N₂ is one molecule made of two nitrogen atoms joined together. Nitrogen gas is an element made of these molecules.
You may have thought a molecule is just another word for an atom. In fact N₂ is a molecule of two nitrogen atoms joined together.

mcqs.q: The symbol Co stands for cobalt. What does CO stand for?
options: Carbon and oxygen atoms joined together
Cobalt, written in capital letters
Carbon and oxygen mixed but not joined
One new atom of carbon and oxygen
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. CO has two capital letters, so it is two symbols: C (carbon) and O (oxygen). It is carbon monoxide, a compound.
rationales: Yes. CO has two capital letters, so it is two symbols: C (carbon) and O (oxygen). It is carbon monoxide, a compound.
You may have thought capital and lower-case letters do not matter. In fact every capital letter starts a new symbol, so CO is carbon and oxygen, not cobalt.
You may have thought a formula just shows elements mixed together. In fact CO is carbon monoxide, a compound: its carbon and oxygen atoms are chemically joined.
You may have thought carbon and oxygen merge into one new kind of atom. In fact CO is a molecule: one carbon atom joined to one oxygen atom, and each atom stays the same atom.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide is CO. Carbon dioxide is CO₂. Which statement is correct?
options: They are one compound in different amounts
CO₂ is two CO molecules joined together
Both molecules have the same number of atoms
CO₂ has one more oxygen atom per molecule
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
mcqs.explain: Yes. CO has 1 carbon and 1 oxygen atom; CO₂ has 1 carbon and 2 oxygen atoms. They are different compounds with different, fixed ratios of atoms.
rationales: You may have thought a compound can contain its elements in any ratio. In fact each compound has a fixed ratio, so CO and CO₂ are two different compounds.
You may have thought the 2 doubles the whole formula. In fact it counts only the oxygen atoms: CO₂ has one carbon atom, not two.
You may have counted symbols, which gives two for each. In fact CO has 2 atoms and CO₂ has 3 atoms.
Yes. CO has 1 carbon and 1 oxygen atom; CO₂ has 1 carbon and 2 oxygen atoms. They are different compounds with different, fixed ratios of atoms.

mcqs.q: Some ice in a sealed bag melts, and a little of the water evaporates. What happens to the mass of the bag and its contents?
options: It goes down, as liquids weigh less than solids
It stays the same, as no particles are lost
It goes up, as ice floats, so water is heavier
It goes down, as water vapour weighs nothing
mcqs.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Melting and evaporating are changes of state: the same water particles are there, just arranged differently. Nothing gets into or out of the sealed bag, so the mass stays the same.
rationales: You may have thought liquids weigh less than solids. In fact the water has exactly the same particles as the ice it came from, so its mass is the same.
Yes. Melting and evaporating are changes of state: the same water particles are there, just arranged differently. Nothing gets into or out of the sealed bag, so the mass stays the same.
You may have thought ice floats because it is lighter. In fact ice floats because it is less dense; the same particles have the same mass, whatever their state.
You may have thought gases have no mass. In fact water vapour has mass, and in a sealed bag it stays inside, so the total mass does not change.

mcqs.q: In an open beaker, 2.0 g of calcium carbonate (chalk) reacts with 50.0 g of acid. Carbon dioxide escapes, and 51.1 g is left. What mass of carbon dioxide escaped?
mcqs.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. The mass at the start was 50.0 + 2.0 = 52.0 g. It fell to 51.1 g, so 52.0 − 51.1 = 0.9 g of carbon dioxide escaped.
mcqs.working: Total mass at the start = 50.0 g + 2.0 g = 52.0 g. Mass lost = 52.0 g − 51.1 g = 0.9 g. The mass lost is the carbon dioxide that escaped into the air.
rationales: You may have thought gases have no mass, so no mass can escape. In fact carbon dioxide has mass: the total fell from 52.0 g to 51.1 g, so 0.9 g escaped.
Yes. The mass at the start was 50.0 + 2.0 = 52.0 g. It fell to 51.1 g, so 52.0 − 51.1 = 0.9 g of carbon dioxide escaped.
You may have left out the chalk and compared 51.1 g with 50.0 g. The starting mass was 50.0 + 2.0 = 52.0 g, so 0.9 g escaped.
You may have thought all the chalk turned into the gas. In fact only some of its atoms leave as carbon dioxide: the mass fell from 52.0 g to 51.1 g, so 0.9 g escaped.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the particles before and after a reaction in a sealed container. What happens to the total mass?
options: It stays the same, as the same atoms are there
It goes down, as there are fewer particles
It goes down, as some atoms were used up
It goes up, as atoms merge into heavier atoms
mcqs.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Count the atoms: two X and four Y before, and two X and four Y after. The same atoms are just joined differently, so the total mass is the same.
rationales: Yes. Count the atoms: two X and four Y before, and two X and four Y after. The same atoms are just joined differently, so the total mass is the same.
You may have counted particles (three before, two after) instead of atoms. Mass depends on the atoms, and there are six atoms both before and after.
You may have thought atoms get used up in a reaction. In fact the diagram shows the same six atoms before and after, just rearranged.
You may have thought the atoms merge into new, heavier atoms. In fact each new particle is an X atom joined to two Y atoms; the atoms themselves have not changed, so neither has the mass.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is heated in a crucible open to the air until it has all turned into white magnesium oxide. None of the powder escapes. What happens to the mass of the crucible and contents?
options: It goes up, as its atoms turn into heavier atoms
It goes down, as some magnesium burns away
It goes up, as oxygen from the air joins on
It stays the same, as oxygen gas has no mass
mcqs.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Magnesium joins with oxygen from the air to make magnesium oxide. The crucible is open, so the mass of that oxygen is added to the reading.
rationales: You may have thought magnesium atoms turn into a new, heavier kind of atom. In fact atoms do not change in reactions; the extra mass is oxygen atoms from the air that joined on.
You may have thought burning makes some of the magnesium vanish. In fact no atoms are destroyed; magnesium atoms join with oxygen from the air, so the mass goes up.
Yes. Magnesium joins with oxygen from the air to make magnesium oxide. The crucible is open, so the mass of that oxygen is added to the reading.
You may have thought a gas joining on cannot add mass. In fact oxygen has mass, and the crucible is open, so the oxygen that joins on adds to the reading.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the particles as sugar dissolves in water. The beaker is on a balance. What happens to the balance reading?
options: It goes down, as the sugar has disappeared
It stays the same, as the sugar is still there
It goes down, as dissolved sugar weighs nothing
It goes up, as the sugary water is denser
mcqs.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Dissolving is not a reaction and no particles are lost: the sugar particles spread out between the water particles. You could get the sugar back by evaporating the water.
rationales: You may have thought dissolved sugar no longer exists because you cannot see it. In fact the sugar particles are still there, spread among the water particles, as the diagram shows.
Yes. Dissolving is not a reaction and no particles are lost: the sugar particles spread out between the water particles. You could get the sugar back by evaporating the water.
You may have thought dissolved sugar is still there but weighs nothing. In fact every sugar particle keeps its mass, so the reading stays the same.
You may have thought a denser liquid must weigh more. In fact the water and sugar were both on the balance before dissolving, and dissolving changes neither the particles nor their mass.

mcqs.q: In Dalton's model, what happens if you keep cutting a piece of copper into smaller and smaller bits?
options: You can keep cutting smaller bits for ever
You reach tiny orange, bendy copper atoms
You reach atoms that cannot be split
You reach atoms visible in a light microscope
mcqs.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
mcqs.explain: Yes. In Dalton's model, matter is made of tiny atoms that cannot be broken down. Cutting stops at single copper atoms.
rationales: You may have thought copper is solid metal all the way through. In fact, in Dalton's model it is made of atoms, and an atom cannot be split.
You may have thought copper atoms are orange and bendy like copper. In fact colour and bendiness belong to a piece of copper, not to one atom.
Yes. In Dalton's model, matter is made of tiny atoms that cannot be broken down. Cutting stops at single copper atoms.
You may have thought the smallest bit you can see is an atom. In fact atoms are far too small to see with a light microscope.

specSource: National Curriculum in England, key stage 3 science — Chemistry; Chemistry — Atoms, elements and compounds (DfE 2013 programme of study, verbatim)

specStatements.text: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

scopeNotes.decision: Dalton's model is tested as a model: atoms are tiny particles that cannot be broken down; in his model all atoms of one element are identical and differ from the atoms of other elements; atoms join in fixed whole-number ratios to make compounds; in reactions atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed; atoms are far too small to see and a single atom does not have the bulk properties of the substance.
scopeNotes.basis: The key stage 3 programme of study names only 'a simple (Dalton) atomic model'. Subatomic particles (protons, neutrons, electrons), the nucleus, isotopes and the development of the model by Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr are GCSE 'atomic structure' content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept, misconception or rationale mentions protons, neutrons, electrons, a nucleus, isotopes, parts inside an atom or any later atomic model. Every claim that the atoms of one element are identical is made as Dalton's ('In Dalton's model …').

scopeNotes.decision: Atoms, elements, molecules and compounds are told apart by whether atoms are of one type or several and whether they are chemically joined; mixtures appear only as the contrast with compounds (not chemically joined, ratio can vary, parts keep their properties).
scopeNotes.basis: Separation techniques and purity belong to the next key stage 3 heading, 'Pure and impure substances'; ionic and covalent bonding and giant structures are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks how to separate a mixture, and none uses the words pure or impure as the tested idea. No item, concept or rationale names ionic bonding, covalent bonding or giant structures; 'joined' and 'chemically bonded' are used without saying how.

scopeNotes.decision: Symbols are one or two letters (capital, then lower case) for common elements, including those that come from Latin names; formulae are read for which elements are present, how many atoms of each and the total, and to tell an element's formula (O₂, N₂) from a compound's (CO₂, CO).
scopeNotes.basis: Working out formulae from ion charges or valency, and brackets in formulae, are GCSE content; naming rules for compounds (-ide, -ate) are not tested in this set; using formulae in equations belongs to the key stage 3 heading 'Chemical reactions'.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every formula in an item, concept, misconception or rationale is one of H₂O, CO₂, CO, NaCl, O₂, N₂, H₂, Cl₂, CH₄, NH₃, CaCO₃, H₂SO₄, Fe₂O₃, MgO, C₆H₁₂O₆ and SO₂ (a number in front, as in 2H₂O or 2N, appears only to contrast it with a subscript), or a generic particle of X and Y atoms in a diagram. No formula contains brackets, and no item uses ion charges, valency or naming rules.

scopeNotes.decision: Total mass is conserved in changes of state, in dissolving and in chemical reactions because the same particles (atoms) are present; in an open container a gas escaping makes the measured mass fall and a gas joining from the air makes it rise; calculations use only addition and subtraction.
scopeNotes.basis: Dissolving is included because the same programme of study lists, under Physics, Matter, Physical changes: 'conservation of material and of mass, and reversibility, in melting, freezing, evaporation, sublimation, condensation, dissolving'. Writing and balancing symbol equations belong to the key stage 3 heading 'Chemical reactions' (and GCSE); amounts in moles and relative formula masses are GCSE content.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks the student to write or balance an equation; atoms are counted only in a reaction shown as a particle diagram. The only mass calculation uses addition and subtraction of masses in grams given to one decimal place, and no item uses moles or relative formula masses.
